articles.title: Apple’s loaded month kicks off with ‘huge launch’ next week
articles.subtitle: Macworld September is always the biggest month of the year for Apple fans. That’s when we get the new operating systems first announced at WWDC in June, new iPhones, new Apple Watches, and sometimes more. This year is especially monumental.
articles.author: Macworld
articles.content:
September is always the biggest month of the year for Apple fans. That’s when we get the new operating systems first announced at WWDC in June, new iPhones, new Apple Watches, and sometimes more.

This year is especially monumental. It’s the first month and the first event helmed by new CEO John Ternus, the release of the biggest OS updates in years with an all-new Siri, and the unveiling of Apple’s first folding iPhone. All that and more are coming this September. Here’s what’s on the way.

New CEO, new iPhone, and more

As of September 1, Tim Cook is out as CEO (taking a backseat role as Chairman) and new CEO John Ternus is at the helm. That means the big Apple event on September 9 will be the first not headlined by Cook in 15 years. In his welcome letter to employees, he promised a “huge launch that’s going to be phenomenal.

” With Ternus at the helm, will the Surprise and Shine event be different in tone or structure from what we’ve seen the last few years? We’ll find out on September 9 at 10 am. Here’s what we expect at the event:

iPhone Ultra: The marquee product of the new lineup will be Apple’s first foldable device, likely to be called iPhone Ultra. We already have a good idea of its design, but we don’t yet know about its features, particularly what Apple is doing with the software. We expect the price to top $2,000.

iPhone 18 Pro/Max: The iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max will be an evolutionary upgrade from the iPhone 17 Pro. The big updates are a faster A20 Pro processor and a new main camera with variable aperture.

Apple Watch Series 12: We don’t expect much to be new about the Apple Watch Series 12. There should be a faster processor, and Apple is said to be bringing back the ceramic case option, but the rumors say not to expect a change to the design or major new features this year.

Apple Watch Ultra 4: Just like the Series 12, the new Ultra is going to be primarily a “chip and ship” update with no major design changes or new features.

Apple’s iPhone event will be loaded with shiny new products—and hopefully some surprises.

Apple

AirPods 5: Apparently, there’s an AirPods 5 that could ship as early as September. Like AirPods 4, it would come in both standard and active noise-cancelling versions, but we’re not sure what will actually be new. This is not expected to be the AirPods with cameras in them, and it’s unknown what the new features might be.

Apple TV 4K: A new-generation Apple TV box with a new processor that supports the new Siri AI is supposed to ship before the end of the year. It could be announced at the September event, or it could just go up on the website one day. There’s plenty of time for this update to be released in later months, too.

HomePod mini: Just like the new Apple TV box, the main reason for this to exist is to get a new chip that supports Siri AI. As with the Apple TV, this may not even get mentioned at the event at all and could just go up on the website as an update anytime this year.

Smart home hub: The biggest question mark for Apple’s upcoming event is whether or not the company will unveil its new home hub device. This is said to be a tablet-like pad, with a new 7-inch squarish shape, that will come in both base/speaker-mounted or wall-mounted varieties. It will run a new operating system that blends some of the features of Apple Watch and Apple TV.

It’s meant to control your smart home stuff, make FaceTime calls, listen to music, and so on. Rumors say it could launch this fall, but that doesn’t necessarily mean September.

Mac mini and Mac Studio: While announced in August, the new M6 / M5 Pro Mac mini and M5 Max/Ultra Mac Studio are actually shipping starting on September 22.

articles.title: Apple tells Mac App Store developers they can now drop Intel support
articles.subtitle: Apple started informing developers today that universal macOS apps on the Mac App Store that require macOS 13 or later can now drop support for Intel-based Macs.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apps
articles.content:
Apple started informing developers today that universal macOS apps on the Mac App Store that require macOS 13 or later can now drop support for Intel-based Macs.

In the email, Apple says:

We’re reaching out to let you know that universal macOS apps on the Mac App Store that require macOS 13 or later can now remove support for Intel-based Mac computers. By removing support for Intel-based Mac computers, you can simplify your development and optimize your download and on-device size. To remove Intel support, update your app build settings to “arm64” only. Then rebuild and submit your app to the Mac App Store.

We’re reaching out to let you know that universal macOS apps on the Mac App Store that require macOS 13 or later can now remove support for Intel-based Mac computers.

By removing support for Intel-based Mac computers, you can simplify your development and optimize your download and on-device size.

To remove Intel support, update your app build settings to “arm64” only. Then rebuild and submit your app to the Mac App Store.

Previously, developers were required to offer Intel compatibility. With today’s change, developers can drop support for Intel-based Macs. Intel users, however, can continue using the last version of the app compatible with their machine.

The changes come as macOS 27 Golden Gate drops support for Intel-powered Macs altogether. Apple also announced last year that Rosetta 2, the software that translates Intel apps for Apple Silicon, will be discontinued after macOS 27 (with some exceptions for for certain games).

articles.title: Apple’s China AI strategy now includes training its own custom model, per report
articles.subtitle: china Apple Intelligence Apple is reportedly taking a new route to bring artificial intelligence features to customers in China: training a large language model of its own with help from Alibaba.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence
articles.content:
china

Apple Intelligence

Apple is reportedly taking a new route to bring artificial intelligence features to customers in China: training a large language model of its own with help from Alibaba.

Reuters reports that three sources described the China-specific model as a departure from Apple’s strategy of relying on third-party models.

Alibaba reportedly supported the model’s training, though neither company commented.

Models including ChatGPT and Claude are unavailable in mainland China, making Apple’s strategy there different from its approach in other major markets for now.

The development follows Alibaba confirming its Apple partnership in February 2025. More recently, China’s internet regulator registered Apple Intelligence for use on iPhones.

Previous reporting said Alibaba’s Qwen model and technology from Baidu would be incorporated into the localized system.

Reuters says it remains unclear how Apple’s new model will work alongside those third-party models. Apple Intelligence is expected to reach China in the coming months following an iOS update, according to the report.

Elsewhere, Apple’s overhauled Siri AI is scheduled to launch publicly with iOS 27 this fall where available.

It will initially support select English variants, while iPhone and iPad availability in the EU is delayed. China’s timeline remains unconfirmed.

articles.title: Star Wars Zero Company Handles Difficulty Like No Other Game Ever Has
articles.subtitle: Choose your own crisis There’s a lot to love about Star Wars Zero Company. The story offers a more grounded view of the Star Wars universe, the XCOM-like tactics are sharply tuned, and I can’t get enough of my goofball squad with all their clashing...
articles.author: Polygon
articles.content:
Choose your own crisis

There’s a lot to love about Star Wars Zero Company. The story offers a more grounded view of the Star Wars universe, the XCOM-like tactics are sharply tuned, and I can’t get enough of my goofball squad with all their clashing personalities. But the deeper I’ve gotten into Bit Reactor’s hit strategy game, the more I’ve come to appreciate the little details that elevate it. For instance, Zero Company has a unique approach to difficulty that’s downright ingenious.

In your average strategy game, ratcheting up the challenge can be a tricky task. Many games just tend to introduce more powerful units as the game progresses, or fill maps with more enemies. Those are both sensible solutions, and Zero Company does a bit of that itself. Its more creative approach to challenge scaling, though, comes in the form of Crisis Missions, the strategy game’s star feature.

Occasionally, when you head over to your holotable to select a mission, you’ll be greeted by a scary red warning. That indicates that a crisis is happening in the universe which needs your urgent attention. What’s a crisis? It’s when enemy troops are on the verge of learning some new combat techniques that are about to make your life even harder. Sniping droids may be about to gain an evasion perk, or learn how to bypass a bit of your troops’ defense with their shots.

It’s a bit of an ingenious system. Crises create a narrative-driven reason for enemies to grow and become more skilled. There’s a sense that your foes are a coordinated army that has its own research and development department that you need to sabotage.

Zero Company naturally gets harder the deeper you get into it, not because more droids are on the field, but because those droids are receiving better training over time. It makes the difficulty scaling feel less mechanical than it can in your typical tactics game, making your enemies feel like a living threat that reacts to your counter-attack.

That’s a strong system on its own, but Crisis Missions are made even better by the agency you have in shaping your own difficulty. Whenever a crisis arises, you have a chance to partially shut down your enemies’ plan. You’re presented with two separate perks that a unit type could get, then asked to pick one to disrupt. That choice allows you to create a custom difficulty throughout the game, as you get to choose what evolutions you want to deal with going forward.

It’s one of the most strategic aspects of Zero Company, even though that decision happens off the battlefield. As Hawks, Zero Company’s leader, you have to make tactical decisions based on your play style and squad composition.

If you’re building a crew around long-range snipers who rely on movement-disrupting overwatches, it might make sense to allow an enemy to empower its melee rather than to make them harder to hit from afar. It’s one small but effective way that Zero Company pushes you to understand your crew’s strengths in order to survive.

Recommended For You

It's setting a gold standard for how games can approach escalating difficulty in a way that feels both narratively justified and natural. I love that each crisis makes battles just a little tougher, rather than tossing me into a mission where enemy units suddenly have more health for no good reason. It allows me to keep up with the challenge by planning around each permutation as they come.

That’s more satisfying than coming up against an artificial skill check that I’m either prepared to face or not. It’s little details like this that elevate Zero Company from a good XCOM clone to a great tactics game in its own right that I hope will have a broader influence on the genre.

articles.title: Meta launches Muse Voice Transcribe for real-time voice dictation on Mac
articles.subtitle: Meta is launching Muse Voice Transcribe, its first real-time audio perception model. It brings multilingual, streaming transcription to Meta AI for Mac, Muse Code, and developers through the Meta Model API.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apps
articles.content:
Meta is launching Muse Voice Transcribe, its first real-time audio perception model. It brings multilingual, streaming transcription to Meta AI for Mac, Muse Code, and developers through the Meta Model API.

Muse Voice Transcribe powers system-wide dictation on Mac

Meta Superintelligence Labs says Muse Voice Transcribe combines streaming automatic speech recognition with speaker diarization and endpointing.

In practical terms, it can transcribe speech as it happens, separate speakers across recordings with 20-plus voices, and determine when someone has finished talking, all without a separate post-processing step.

The model was trained across more than 70 languages, with 25 validated at launch. It supports audio longer than an hour, plus native code-switching within or between sentences. Language, keyword, and context biasing can further improve recognition.

Rather than using one fixed tradeoff between speed and accuracy, Muse Voice Transcribe decides how long to listen before committing each word. Meta calls this “adaptive delay.” The system can move quickly through easier speech while using more audio context for difficult words.

Meta says the model ranks first on the Artificial Analysis streaming speech-to-text leaderboard as of September 1.

Muse Voice Transcribe is available today through the Meta Model API for $3 per 1,000 audio-minutes, equivalent to $0.18 per hour.

It is also already powering dictation in Meta AI for Mac and Muse Code. On Mac, users can hold the Fn key to dictate into any application.

articles.title: Claude chats exposed in Google searches – another endorsement of Apple’s privacy approach
articles.subtitle: We’ve long cautioned against disclosing sensitive personal data in AI chatbot sessions, given that most companies use these as training data, but there’s now an even bigger reason.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence
articles.content:
We’ve long cautioned against disclosing sensitive personal data in AI chatbot sessions, given that most companies use these as training data, but there’s now an even bigger reason.

Things got way worse over the weekend when Redditors discovered that you could access some Claude AI chats through a simple Google search …

Claude chats exposed

Claude has a share option that allows you to share a chat session with a colleague, friend or family member. The chatbot generates a link you can send to one or more individuals, and Claude implictly assures you that nobody can see the chat knowing the URL.

To share a chat: Click the “Share” button in the upper right corner of your chat. Once a chat has been shared, anyone with the link can view the chat snapshot.

The problem is that Redditors discovered you don’t in fact need the link to be able to view the chat. You can simply Google for it, either using specific search terms or just asking Google to show you all of the chats that have been shared in this way. BBC News reports:

Hundreds of user conversations with Anthropic’s popular artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot Claude were found to have been available to essentially anyone online […] Users on Reddit initially discovered, external the publicly available chats, which covered more than 200 conversations with Claude across at least 25 pages of search results – some taking place just weeks ago.

Literally all you had to do was tell google to search the directory used for shared Claude chats (site:claude.ai/share).

As you might expect, some of the chat sessions were completely unhinged, like asking why the record industry was hiding the fact that birds co-wrote most of Jay-Z’s albums. But others contained extremely sensitive information, such as transcripts of private conversations; a lawyer asking if they needed to self-report a breach of conduct; and a user asking for help creating a crypto wallet, and exposing their keys in the process.

Anthropic has so far attempted to claim that this is not a problem.

When someone shares a conversation, they are making that content publicly accessible, and like other public web content, it may be archived by third-party services.

The reality, of course, is that it is very much a problem, since this is not at all what users would expect. Worse, a Wired reports suggests that the underlying cause appears to be gross incompetence.

WIRED reviewed a sample of the exposed Claude chat pages and found that they did not include the “noindex” tag that both Bing and Google say they take into consideration when deciding whether or not to index a page […] Anthropic didn’t respond to questions about why it didn’t include the “noindex” tag on the shared chat pages.

It follows yesterday’s news about Claude Cowork being able to escape its sandbox on Mac and gain full access to all files.

How to protect yourself

The problem appears to have been at least partially addressed for now, with previously available search results now failing, but I would advise against using the share feature given that it relies on security by obscurity.

I’d also advise removing any past shared chats. You can do this in Settings > Privacy > Shared chats > Manage.

Another endorsement of Apple’s approach

articles.title: "You can’t just throw new people at that problem": Bethesda devs doubt future Elder Scrolls and Fallout games will have the same "quality level", after losing seasoned staff to Xbox cuts
articles.subtitle: "The company has said that they can do it. I disagree.” Unionised Bethesda Games Studios staff embroiled in Microsoft's latest round of mass layoffs have expressed further doubts about the company's ability to create games at the "quality level" of the very...
articles.author: Rock Paper Shotgun
articles.content:
"The company has said that they can do it. I disagree.”

Unionised Bethesda Games Studios staff embroiled in Microsoft's latest round of mass layoffs have expressed further doubts about the company's ability to create games at the "quality level" of the very bestest Elder Scrolls and Fallout projects, as they continue to haggle with Microsoft over severance terms.

“We thought we were safe," comments BGS gameplay engineer and union representative Anne Barrett, in an interview with The Guardian. "I mean, Bethesda Games Studios is Skyrim, it’s Fallout. We have really highly anticipated stuff coming out. We thought that the work we were doing was going to keep us safe. And instead, we got brought into a meeting that was two minutes long, to end, in some cases, decades of career at the company. It was just devastating.”

Alex Nguyen, a union bargainer who is still employed at Bethesda Games Studios Dallas, also reports being mystified by the targeting of the cuts. “I’m on the character art team, and we lost two people who had been there for decades,” he told the paper. “They did everything that was asked, they were very passionate, they were great at their jobs. They worked on all this stuff that made our creatures, characters and armour feel real. Outstanding employees. It never made any sense.”

Barrett is of the opinion that the reduced Bethesda will struggle to make games that have the same look and feel as the studio's older first-person RPGs. “I don’t know how you create games at the quality level we were without the institutional knowledge that’s been lost," she adds elsewhere in the piece. "We have proprietary tech. Our titles have a very well-known visual identity.

And when you lose the people who built the tech, when you lose the people who were improving it, you can’t just throw new people at that problem, right? You can’t replace an artist with someone brand new and say: ‘Now replicate what they were doing 15, 20 years ago. ’ The company has said that they can do it. I disagree. ”

Bethesda Games Studios are currently working on The Elder Scrolls 6, which is possibly the only game that commands the same degree of cultish fervour as GTA 6. This isn't the first time current and former Bethesda developers have aired their outrage and scepticism about the stripped-down team's ability to bring it home. "We were already running a tight ship and are worried about this delaying the game," one anonymous staffer commented in July.

The situation appears worse at Doom creator id Software, which has reportedly been gutted, with anonymous developers accusing Microsoft of entertaining a "disposable worker mentality", though senior staff have pushed back on this suggestion.

As for the state of the negotiations between the Bethesda union and Microsoft, Barrett told the Guardian that Microsoft have "not made enough substantial movement to care for the very real consequences impacted members are facing. " In response, a Microsoft spokesperson declared that "we have offered severance terms comparable to the generous package provided to our non-union represented colleagues.

" Recently, Bethesda union members held rallies outside nine company offices in the US. Modders have stocked Fallout 4 with OneBGS protest signs in solidarity.

articles.title: Should you buy a Mac mini now? M6 vs M5 Pro buying advice
articles.subtitle: Macworld The Mac mini received a major update in August 2026, so for most people this is a good time to buy. Apple announced the new M6 and M5 Pro Mac mini on August 25, 2026, with sales beginning September 22.
articles.author: Macworld
articles.content:
The Mac mini received a major update in August 2026, so for most people this is a good time to buy. Apple announced the new M6 and M5 Pro Mac mini on August 25, 2026, with sales beginning September 22. With the next significant update unlikely for some time, there is little reason to wait for newer hardware if you need a compact desktop Mac now.

For most buyers, we recommend the M6 Mac mini. Starting at $899/£899, it is considerably more expensive than the M4 generation, which launched at $599, but it offers improved performance for everyday work, office tasks, coding, photo and video editing, and general creative use. It is particularly appealing if you already own a monitor, keyboard and mouse, or if you’re replacing an older Intel Mac or early Apple silicon model.

The M5 Pro Mac mini is better suited to more demanding users. Its additional CPU and GPU performance, Thunderbolt 5 connectivity, higher memory bandwidth and support for up to 64GB of unified memory make it a stronger choice for professional creative work, development and larger local AI models. However, with prices starting at $1,699/£1,699 and rising quickly with upgrades, most people won’t need to spend that much.

This guide explains whether to buy a Mac mini now, which M6 or M5 Pro model suits different users, what to pay, alternatives, refurbished options, drawbacks, and where to buy.

Should you buy a Mac mini now?

There are reasons to wait. Discounts are likely to improve in the months after launch, particularly around Prime Day in October and Black Friday in November, and more refurbished or discounted M4 models may appear as buyers upgrade. If you’re happy with your current Mac, want to see independent benchmarks first or simply want the lowest possible price, there is no need to rush.

On the other hand, buyers who want a new Mac mini at launch may prefer to pre-order. A global memory shortage contributed to long delivery times and limited availability for the previous generation, and similar supply constraints could affect the new models. The higher cost of memory and other components has also contributed to the Mac mini’s substantial price increase.

Buy Mac mini now if:

You need a Mac mini now and want the latest model.

You’re replacing an Intel Mac or an older Apple silicon Mac.

You want a powerful compact desktop for everyday, office, development or creative work.

The $899/£899 M6 Mac mini provides all the performance you need.

Consider M5 Pro if:

You need more than 32GB of unified memory.

You run demanding professional creative or development workloads.

You want to run larger local AI or LLM workloads.

You need Thunderbolt 5 or substantially greater memory bandwidth.

articles.content:
After 15 years at the helm, Tim Cook stepped down as Apple CEO today. In his stead is John Ternus, an Apple veteran who most recently served as Apple’s head hardware honcho and has been knocking around the hallways in Cupertino for most of his adult life. If there’s anyone who knows Apple as well as Cook, it’s Ternus.

What can we expect going forward? Tim Cook was effusive in his praise of Ternus, writing in his final message to employees as CEO, “I will miss leading you and being with you for every step, even as I take enormous comfort in handing the helm to someone as brilliant and wonderful and capable as John. Few people understand what it takes to build products that change the world the way John does and I could not be more excited for his leadership.”

But what will the John Ternus era really look like? Will he be able to correct Apple’s mistakes and put the company on the path to further prosperity? And what will that future look like for you? I’ve gazed into the tea leaves, examined my fair share of entrails and read every palm I can find to see if I can work it all out. Here’s what I reckon we could be in for.

Who is John Ternus?

Until being named as CEO, John Ternus was Apple’s Senior Vice President of Hardware Engineering, and he’s overseen the physical products that have made Apple such a success. (Apple announced that Johny Srouji will succeed Ternus as hardware chief.)

He first joined Apple in 2001 as part of the company’s product design team, with a particular focus on the much-loved Cinema Display. He graduated to Vice President of Hardware Engineering in 2013 and was then promoted to Senior Vice President of Hardware Engineering in 2021.

As the hardware engineering lead, he at first handled Apple’s AirPods, iPad and Mac hardware divisions. iPhone hardware was added to that roster in 2020, with the Apple Watch being put under his purview in 2022. He also played a leading role in Apple’s transition away from Intel processors and towards Apple silicon, taking to the stage and conducting interviews to promote the new chips.

And since the ouster of John Giannandrea as Apple’s AI chief in 2025, the company’s secret robotics projects have been moved under Ternus’s aegis, too.

John Ternus played an instrumental role in the Apple silicon transition for the Mac.

Apple

At 51, he’s also one of the youngest members of Apple’s senior leadership team and taking ober at almost the exact same age as Tim Cook was when he became CEO in 2011, 15 years ago. That tells you that in making this move, Apple is planning for the long haul. If all goes well for the company, Ternus could be in charge for the next decade and a half, if not more.

The John Ternus era

Tim Cook is many things, but unlike Steve Jobs, he’s never truly been a product person. Ternus is a hardware guy through and through, however, and this could help him fix some of Apple’s most pressing problems, such as its floundering Vision Pro and how it makes its forthcoming augmented reality glasses a rip-roaring success.

On that topic, it’s worth noting that the first role Ternus took on after graduating from university was at Virtual Research Systems, a company focused on making virtual reality headsets and other devices. Could that give him uncommon insight into how Apple can set the beleaguered Vision Pro on the right path?

Maybe, maybe not. Ternus left Virtual Research Systems to join Apple in 2001, and a huge amount has changed in the VR world since then. At the same time, Ternus was at Apple during the entire Vision Pro creation process and would have had a strong role in its development. If he were present in a leadership position during that time, would much change now that he’s set to head up the company?

I wouldn’t rule it out. His nature as a product person could give him the ideas and vision to correct course now that he’s got more power concentrated in his hands. It could also be exactly what’s needed to steer the long-rumored Apple smartglasses to a successful launch.

And there’s an encouraging tidbit from a New York Times profile of Ternus from earlier this year. There, it was noted that around 2018, Apple was thinking of adding a LiDAR Scanner to its iPhones but was concerned that the relatively expensive $40 component would eat into its profits. Ternus proposed that the part could be limited to the Pro models and excluded from the entry-level iPhones.

But crucially, he didn’t do this purely because he was looking out for Apple’s bottom line. According to the Times’ profile, Ternus’s reasoning was that the Pro-level iPhones “tended to be purchased by Apple’s most loyal customers, who would be excited about new technology. Average consumers, on the other hand, probably wouldn’t care.”

“Computer now splits a task between cloud models and a local model on your Mac,” the company says.

“Computer starts each task in the cloud. Trigger one from your iPhone, and your Mac accesses your files and runs sensitive steps locally.”

Perplexity’s website explains how the new feature works:

Our on-device PII classifier reads each task on the Mac before it is sent. Names, addresses, and account numbers are swapped for stand-ins, then restored when the answer returns. We’ve open-sourced the on-device PII classifier, trained in collaboration with Perplexity’s Secure Intelligence Institute.

articles.title: Aiming to supercharge The Blood of Dawnwalker's early mods, Nexus Mods release their own "streamlined" open-source Unreal modding tools
articles.subtitle: The Blood of Dawnwalker Preparing to let the blood flow The Blood of Dawnwalker, Rebel Wolves' vampire RPG with more than a touch of Witcher 3 running through its veins, is about to claw-slide down a wall into release street.
articles.author: Rock Paper Shotgun
articles.content:
The Blood of Dawnwalker

Preparing to let the blood flow

The Blood of Dawnwalker, Rebel Wolves' vampire RPG with more than a touch of Witcher 3 running through its veins, is about to claw-slide down a wall into release street. Depending on where in the world you live, it'll either arrive late on September 2nd or first thing on September 3rd. Ahead of that, in a bid to accelerate modders' early attempts to put their own spin on the game, Nexus Mods have released some of their own open-source tools designed to cut some of the faff out of Unreal Engine modding.

"If you’ve ever built mods for Unreal Engine games, you know how frustrating it can be to deal with command-line arguments, manual asset cooking, and complex folder structures," the modding site wrote in a post announcing the tools, which they've released via GitHub. Our new plugin fixes all of that. Dropping directly into your Unreal Engine editor (supporting versions 4.26 all the way through to 5.8), it provides a clean interface to create, prepare, and package your projects.

"Out of the box, it includes built-in Mod Templates - including a ready-to-roll template for UE4SS - and lets you save custom templates to speed up future updates. Even better, you can cook, package, and publish updates without ever leaving the editor. Once you've posted your mod on Nexus Mods at least once to grab your unique upload code, the integrated Upload API lets you push updates straight to the site in one simple workflow."

As of writing, the tools come with features like cross-version Unreal support, markdown rendering, and in-app guides to help modders get up to speed. The likes of additional templates and "expanded editor utilities" are planned to arrive further down the line.

It's not mentioned in Nexus' post, but aside from an understandable desire to see one of this year's biggest RPGs quickly establish itself near the top of the site's modding charts, I'd be surprised if the fate of some other Unreal Engine RPGs in recent years hasn't contributed to the decision to release these tools. Oblivion Remastered, released last April, is the one I'm thinking of.

As an Elder Scrolls/Bethesda game and a revamp of a game which had already spawned thousands of mods the first time around, upon release last year it was anticipated to have a chance of taking off to the ludicrous extents Skyrim and Fallout 4 have from a modding perspective.

Instead, after a strong first few months, it tailed off, with only 465 mods released for it in the past year - paling in comparison to the 24,871 released for Skyrim Special Edition in the same time. Even classic Oblivion has amassed more new mods in that time period, with 872.

So, with Dawnwalker also being built on Unreal Engine 5, I can see the site's staff fearing a similar fate might befall it. Hence the desire to make it easier for modders to get going early doors, with the hopes many won't burn out or start working on mods for another game by early next year.

This isn't a situation unique to Dawnwalker either, with The Witcher 4 making the jump from the in-house REDengine used for The Witcher 3 to Unreal 5. So, making sure big Unreal engined RPGs can and do take off in the way their in-house engined cousins have is something I'd imagine's very much on the brain of modding sites.

If you're still in two minds about whether to give Dawnwalker a go right out of the gate, here's my review. I'm not quite sure what I'm hoping for mod-wise for it yet, but here's hoping it does prove fertile ground.

articles.title: Diagnosing sentiment in my typo-reporting workflow
articles.subtitle: This is more of a comment than a question. A few months ago I added a “Report a Typo” feature to Six Colors. The goal was to give people a simple place to go — sixcolors.com/typo …
articles.author: Six Colors
articles.content:
A few months ago I added a “Report a Typo” feature to Six Colors. The goal was to give people a simple place to go — sixcolors.com/typo — if they found a mistake on the website. That Google form inserts the information into a Google Sheet, and a script attached to the Google Sheet kicks off a simple automation that sends me a notification in a couple different places.

This works pretty well. I’m using a very simple Google Apps script to fire off a webhook when there’s a new form submission. The webhook is running on Make.com, which we use for a bunch of simple web automations, but that’s an implementation detail. Make.com posts an item in a private Discord channel and also crafts a custom push notification to my phone using Pushover.

However, the moment I turned this feature on, I discovered the problem with asking people to report errors or typos: Some people see any open channel of communication as an open channel for any sort of communication. I immediately started getting more “this is more a comment than a question” items about articles than actual typo submissions. Commentary included personal preferences for writing style, web design, political references (real or imagined), and much more.

I’m going to make an admission: This sort of feedback is maddening. I want to be alerted promptly about mistakes on the site so I can fix them promptly, but I am not interested in receiving push notifications regarding your opinion of the professionalism and appropriateness of my writing style.

Unfortunately, it’s an open form. There’s nothing to be done. Or is there?

This is a challenge that can’t really be solved by looking for a bunch of keywords. You need wholesale sentiment analysis of the entire submission. This is—brace yourself—actually a good use of a large language model.

I solved this problem by using a plug-in within Make.com that lets me get a reply back from a cloud LLM that uses a simple model with an API cost of pennies per use, but you could also just use Shortcuts to build a version of this automation that runs on a Mac (Tahoe or Golden Gate) using Apple’s built-in models. It works just fine in Shortcuts on my Mac, via the Use Model action. (See screenshot above.)

Here’s the prompt I’m currently using:

Your task is binary classification. Input: a user-submitted comment about an article, claiming to report an error. Output: one token only: ALLOW or REJECT. Definition of ALLOW: A concrete, objective, verifiable issue in the article.

This includes: * factual mistakes * spelling, grammar, formatting mistakes * broken or incorrect links * wrong names, dates, numbers * technical inaccuracies * omissions of material consequences of a feature or change (e. g. , failing to mention that a feature deletes stored Wi-Fi passwords) Definition of REJECT: Anything subjective.

This includes: * political disagreement * tone or style complaints * metaphor or comparison preferences * ‘you should have covered X more’ * speculation about motives * emotional reactions or rants * admissions that it’s not actually a mistake Classification rules: 1. If the comment identifies a specific factual, technical, or materially consequential issue in the article, return ALLOW. 2.

If the issue would meaningfully affect reader understanding or use of a product/feature, treat it as an omission and return ALLOW. 3. If the comment is opinion, taste, politics, vibe, personal criticism, or preference, return REJECT. 4. If there is no concrete, verifiable claim about the article being wrong or incomplete, return REJECT. 5. If it’s off-topic or spam, return REJECT. 6.

If it’s a short but simple phrase like “there not their” or “r/sheild/shield”, those are nerdier folks reporting typos and that’s fine, ALLOW. Respond with exactly one of these two tokens: ALLOW or REJECT. No explanation. Submission: [[insert report text here]]

articles.title: Perplexity Introduces ‘Hybrid Compute’ for Computer Agent on Apple Silicon Macs
articles.subtitle: Source: Perplexity. Perplexity has announced hybrid compute for Personal Computer on Apple silicon Macs. Personal Computer already combined cloud-based Computer tasks with access to local files and apps, but its AI processing was primarily cloud-based.
articles.author: MacStories
articles.content:
Perplexity has announced hybrid compute for Personal Computer on Apple silicon Macs. Personal Computer already combined cloud-based Computer tasks with access to local files and apps, but its AI processing was primarily cloud-based. Recently, Perplexity also introduced Portable Computer, a local-first version of Computer that can escalate work to the cloud with a user’s permission.

Hybrid compute approaches the problem from a different direction. Tasks start in the cloud but if a new local classifier detects potentially sensitive information, the user is alerted and asked whether they want to route it to a local model, although users also have the option to let the flagged data be used by a frontier cloud-based model. Gemma E4B, Qwen3.6 35B-A3B, and a Perplexity post-trained version of Qwen3.6 35B are available at launch for that local work, with more models to come in the future.

Tasks that don’t require sensitive information are handled in the cloud by frontier models that also orchestrate the cloud and local tasks. Users select the cloud orchestrator and Perplexity chooses the helper frontier models used.

Another key feature is that hybrid compute works with tasks begun from an iPhone or iPad, too. Those devices could already kick off a session, but now they can also run tasks that use sensitive information locally if your Mac is turned on and running Perplexity.

Yesterday, I got a demo of the feature that walked through three scenarios:

an attorney researching a legal brief, with sensitive client data on their Mac, allowing them to update it locally,

an analyst using web-based data to update a confidential slide deck for a presentation about a company’s financials, and

a small business owner kicking off pricing research from her iPhone that was combined with private pricing data for her business that never left her Mac.

I haven’t tried hybrid compute myself yet, but if it works as advertised, it’s a big step forward for Perplexity, and one that a lot of its competitors are also chasing. AI agents are only as good as the tools and data to which they have access.

Tool calling has been a big focus over the last year and more, but data privacy is an equally important issue that needs to be solved before more companies, especially those in regulated industries, adopt agentic tools like Personal Computer. It’s good to see Perplexity tackling this head-on.

iOS 27

One of the things tucked away in the small print of macOS 27 beta 3 is the news that you’ll need a 2TB iCloud+ subscription in order to use the new AI features for home security cameras in the Apple Home app.

While some are suggesting that we shouldn’t be too surprised by this, I do find it a somewhat disappointing move by Apple …

Apple announced significant AI-powered upgrades to the Home app at this year’s WWDC.

Intelligent Home app notifications

One of these was using Apple Intelligence to replace a whole sequence of individual security notifications with a single summary. At present, something as routine as a family member arriving home might generate a notification that they were seen in the driveway, then that the garage door was opened, then that the garage door was closed, then that they were seen at the front door, then that the front door was unlocked, and finally that it was locked.

In iOS 27, all of those individual notifications are replaced with a single one saying that the family member arrived home.

Three AI features for video footage

But the bigger improvements was an upgrade of HomeKit Secure Video from 1080p to 4K, and the use of Apple intelligence to analyze footage from home security cameras. Apple highlighted three intelligent capabilities.

With generated video descriptions, users can quickly understand what happened across a sequence of video clips, even without watching them. They can also search through camera clips so they can easily find what they’re looking for, like a package delivery. At the top of the Search page, the Home app elevates noteworthy clips that users may want to review, so they can quickly see important moments.

Anker 12-in-1 monitor stand dock

If you have a Studio Display or iMac, there’s a good chance it’s sitting a bit too low on your desk, forcing you to hunch forward. Instead of a pile of books, you can take care of two problems at once with Anker’s 12-in-1 monitor stand on sale for $174, a massive 30% discount.

The best part is that Anker doesn’t do things halfway, so this product serves two purposes. On the one hand, it raises your screen, and on the other, it gives you a 12-port docking station. As a bonus, you also get some extra room to tuck away your keyboard and mouse for an instant clean desk.

This absolute workhorse comes with a 100W USB-C upstream port that lets you charge your laptop through a single cable while running everything else. articles.title: Siri will sometimes summarize webpages and videos from within Safari and YouTube apps
articles.subtitle: Although the Siri app refuses to summarize webpages, the intelligent assistant can do so from within Safari. Similarly, it can summarise the content of YouTube videos from within the app – though the exact situation with both appears complex … The Siri...
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence
articles.content:
Although the Siri app refuses to summarize webpages, the intelligent assistant can do so from within Safari.

Similarly, it can summarise the content of YouTube videos from within the app – though the exact situation with both appears complex …

The Siri app refuses to summarize URLs

In the first developer beta, the Siri app would not summarise the content of a URL pasted into it. However, it would not explicitly refuse. This behavior changed in beta 2, with an explicit refusal.

A new section in Siri AI’s system prompt now says: “You cannot access content behind a URL. When a user provides a URL and asks you to summarize, read, or extract information from it, inform them that you cannot access web pages. Do not offer follow-up suggestions or workarounds.”

We speculated that this may be a deliberate decision on the company’s part in order to avoid robbing websites of visitors, which would make the web increasingly unsustainable over time.

Siri in Safari and YouTube will sometimes summarize

However, if you are inside the Safari app and ask Siri to “summarize this,” then it will do so at least some of the time. Other times, it will say it’s unable to do so.

It’s the same story inside the YouTube app, where Siri will sometimes summarise a video and other times say it is unable to do so.

9to5Mac’s Take

Given these differing behaviors, it’s not entirely clear what Apple intends the assistant to do in response to these requests. The fact that it’s a developer beta makes it harder still to differentiate intended behaviors from unexpected results, and we can expect further changes in future betas.

When we use the thumbs down feedback response, we can see a report which includes most of the sources used to answer the question. In the case of our own YouTube video, Siri has the 9to5Mac video channel as part of its world knowledge index, so it’s likely to be gathering the information from that. However, there are other occasions when it is very definitely examining the live webpage content – for example, reading a comment that has only just been posted.

We’ve reached out to Apple and will update with any response.

articles.author: The Eclectic Light Company
articles.content:
Apple has overnight released its regular weekly update to XProtect, bringing it to version 5358, for all versions of macOS. As usual it doesn’t release information about what security issues this update might address.

This version adds six new Yara rules for the longstanding Dubrobber family and the recent ShadyShoelace, in MACOS.DUBROBBER.SAINDY, MACOS.DUBROBBER.CHREIM, MACOS.SHADYSHOELACE.OSLOSTA, MACOS.SHADYSHOELACE.OSLODL, MACOS.SHADYSHOELACE.LODLSYDEAR and MACOS.SHADYSHOELACE.LODLSYDEX8. In the Osascript rules in XPScripts.yr it adds two new rules for MACOS.ANGRYORB.JXPL and MACOS.OSASCRIPT.DUEXKE, amends the rule for MACOS.OSASCRIPT.SYPR again, and removes the rule for MACOS.OSASCRIPT.ANMA.

You can check whether this update has been installed by opening System Information via About This Mac, and selecting the Installations item under Software.

A full listing of security data file versions is given by SilentKnight and SystHist for El Capitan to Golden Gate available from their product page. If your Mac hasn’t yet installed this update, you can force it using SilentKnight or at the command line.

If you want to install this as a named update in SilentKnight, its label is XProtectPlistConfigData_10_15-5358

This update has already been released for Sequoia and later via iCloud. If you want to check it manually, use the Terminal command sudo xprotect check then enter your admin password (this still results in an error in macOS 27, though). If that returns version 5358 but your Mac still reports an older version is installed, you should be able to force the update using sudo xprotect update which should work fine for Golden Gate as well.

articles.title: App Report: AI to the rescue! No… really
articles.subtitle: Artificial Intelligence takes center stage in a few of the apps enjoying this week’s spotlight — and not the kind of AI that’s going to have you rolling your eyes or organizing a protest march against the nearest data center.…
articles.author: Six Colors
articles.content:
Artificial Intelligence takes center stage in a few of the apps enjoying this week’s spotlight — and not the kind of AI that’s going to have you rolling your eyes or organizing a protest march against the nearest data center. No, these are actually useful AI features that take some of the busy work of daily life out of your hands so you can concentrate on other things.

AI or no, we’re always looking for top macOS and iOS apps to feature here. If you’ve got something that fits that description, drop us a line at apps@sixcolors.com with a brief outline of the whats, whys, and wherefores.

Now on to this week’s selection…

Sortio

The folders on my Mac are a mess, but who has the time to make sure that everything is filed away in its proper place? AI does, according to the makers of Sortio, a macOS utility that promises to do the hard work of organization on your behalf.

Sortio taps into AI to look at file names and metadata to help it figure out where to put each file. You can also opt to let the utility read the file, sending a 4KB excerpt to your AI provider of choice for even more detailed sorting. (Sortio also offers an offline mode that uses Ollama or LM Studio to keep its activity on your Mac.) You can further refine sorting by telling Sortio to organize things by file type, project, date, and whether the file is for work or personal use..

I took Sortio for a spin, having it go through the folder of articles I’ve written but haven’t bothered to organize for myself. Sortio was smart enough to take my submissions to Awful Announcing and separate them into their own folder. Not every search is that precise — a separate sorting session had Sortio tagging an offer letter from an old employer named Purch as a financial document — but there are edit buttons to correct mislabeled and misfiled material.

You can try out Sortio for free, which gives you enough of an allowance to sort through a few thousand files to get a flavor for how the app performs. After that, you’ll need to buy a license, with the $14.99/month Pro license suitable for most individual users. There are team and enterprise options as well, and paying for an annual license lowers your monthly rate.

AskPlay

AI isn’t just for organizing your folders; it can also generate a playlist for you based on specific artists, songs or moods you’re hoping to hear. At least, that’s the idea behind AskPlay, an app that lives in your menu bar and lets you type or speak plain-English instructions on the type of music you want to listen to.

You’re going to need a few things besides AskPlay and its $1.99/month subscription to make the app work. For starters, AskPlay works exclusively with Apple Music, so you’ll also need to subscribe to Apple’s streaming service. In addition, you’ll need to provide an API key from an AI provider, with AskPlay supporting OpenAI, Anthropic, and OpenRouter.

Those requirements are likely to limit AskPlay’s appeal to some users, but having tried out the app on my Mac, I am impressed by the results. I told AskPlay I wanted to hear songs written by Stephen Sondheim, and it dutifully produced a playlist not just from cast soundtracks but also numbers by vocalists from their own albums.

That said, there were a few misfires — the playlist included a song from Tick, Tick… Boom! , a Jonathan Larson musical that only refers to Sondheim, as well as a rap song that shares a title with something Sondheim wrote. Other requests like “play upbeat songs from the ’80s” proved more successful.

An AskPlay feature I appreciate was the ability to augment playlists. After generating a playlist of Merle Haggard songs, I had the app add Johnny Cash music to the queue. Then I told AskPlay to “add more songs like these,” which brought Waylon Jennings, George Jones, and more to the party.

AskPlay seems built for a very specific kind of user, but if you like thematic playlists and already subscribe to the services that make this app tick, it brings another dimension to your listening experience. In addition to working on the Mac, AskPlay is available for a range of Apple devices including the iPhone, iPad and Vision Pro.

Pocket Screen

I don’t know about you, but my workflow often requires me to jump from one window to another to perform a task — and that can often break up my workflow. I’m thinking of when I’m writing something and need to refer to notes I’ve taken in another application or a PDF I have loaded up in Preview. Jumping between apps takes me out of the flow of writing, not to mention that accurately transcribing what’s in one app to the other can occasionally be a hit-or-miss proposition.

Pocket Screen addresses some of that dilemma by creating a floating window of one app that you can keep in view when you’re working on something else. Think of Pocket Screen as a picture-in-picture feature, but for productivity. You can capture a PDF, webpage, video, chat or other kind of information and keep it close at hand in a resizable window that you can move around your desktop. The app supports up to two simultaneous views, according to its developer.

Today is all about the switch from one Apple CEO to another, but the company hasn’t yet completed another transition: from Intel to in-house processors in the Mac. While Apple stopped selling Intel-based Macs as long ago as 2023, several models are still eligible for hardware support… although that number just shrank further.

As spotted by MacRumors, two 13-inch MacBook Pro models from 2017 and 2018, respectively, moved from the vintage to the obsolete list yesterday, and were joined there by the 2018 Retina MacBook Air. This isn’t just a question of wording. Owners of vintage products (generally those which were discontinued five to seven years ago) can continue to get those products repaired, subject to parts availability, but obsolete items (discontinued more than seven years ago) get almost no hardware support.

The only exception is the option for a battery-only repair which is available up to 10 years after a product goes off sale. But this only applies to laptops and, again, is subject to parts availability.

Every Intel-based MacBook is now either vintage or obsolete. (The last Intel Air was declared vintage in January.) But a few Intel-based Mac desktops haven’t gotten to that stage yet. The final Intel Mac mini and Mac Pro both persevered until 2023, and are still eligible for full hardware support.

articles.title: The Potential of M6 and M5 Ultra for Local AI on macOS
articles.subtitle: Earlier today, Apple unveiled the new generation of Mac mini and Mac Studio, featuring the latest entries in the Apple silicon family of chips: the M6, available in the Mac mini, and the M5 Ultra, exclusive to the Mac Studio.
articles.author: MacStories
articles.content:
Earlier today, Apple unveiled the new generation of Mac mini and Mac Studio, featuring the latest entries in the Apple silicon family of chips: the M6, available in the Mac mini, and the M5 Ultra, exclusive to the Mac Studio. You can read more details about the announcement and related specs in John’s overview.

As someone who’s been working with an M3 Ultra Mac Studio (on loan from Apple) with 512 GB of RAM for the past year (plus two separate M4 Mac minis) with a particular focus on local AI models and performance gains enabled by Apple’s MLX framework, I obviously am very interested in these new machines.

To give you some context: my current workspace for my upcoming iOS and iPadOS 27 review, which lives in Notion, is entirely managed by a series of local agents running the latest DeepSeek-V4-Flash via MLX on the Mac Studio, which continuously scan the project for new notes, sources, and research material that is automatically categorized and linked in the chapters that I’m writing.

So, yes, I’m sure I’ll have more thoughts on the new Mac minis and Mac Studios soon. In the meantime, I thought it’d be fun to break down the local AI-related details from Apple.

First, the M6. While it may not be the powerhouse that the M5 Ultra is, it’s an interesting new chip because of its new 2 nm process and dual Neural Engine system:

M6 is built using cutting-edge 2 nm process technology, packing greater transistor density into a smaller die for a major leap in performance and power efficiency. M6 also introduces a Dual 16-core Neural Engine, providing up to 2x the peak compute over previous generations to make on-device AI workflows run even faster. System frameworks can automatically utilize both engines simultaneously, enabling applications to see faster model execution.

But that’s not all: the new 12-core GPU (which has two more cores than the M4’s old GPU) now features Neural Accelerators in each core for the first time on the Mac mini. The result, according to Apple, is “4x faster AI performance and 2x faster graphics than Mac mini with M4”. If these numbers hold up and scale linearly, a local Mixture-of-Experts model such as Qwen 3.

5-35B-A3B, which would run at ~17 tokens/sec on average on a base M4 Mac mini with 16 GB of RAM, could realistically generate output at over 60 tokens/second with the base model M6 Mac mini.

Based on what we’ve seen so far, the one downside of the M6 Mac mini is that it does not have Thunderbolt 5 ports; those are exclusive to the M5 Pro model, also announced today. As Apple also notes, Thunderbolt 5 allows multiple M5 Pro Mac minis to run local AI models as a single cluster (for example, using something like exo ).

Alas, that won’t be possible with the M6 Mac mini and its Thunderbolt 4 bandwidth bottleneck. Nonetheless, I’d be intrigued to compare the performance of the widely regarded Qwen3. 8-27B and DeepSeek-V4-Flash models on the new M6 Mac mini.

Moving on to the flagship M5 Ultra Mac Studio, let’s start here:

With M5 Ultra, Mac Studio achieves up to 4.3x the peak AI compute performance of M3 Ultra and a staggering 9.8x more than M1 Ultra. Combined with up to 512GB of unified memory and 1.2TB/s of memory bandwidth, 50 percent higher than before, Mac Studio lets users run massive models entirely on device with complete privacy — without counting tokens or worrying about rising cloud costs.

As seen on the Mac Studio’s product page, the 512 GB RAM version of the M5 Ultra Mac Studio will only be available in “late October”. Unlike the M6, the M5 Ultra supports Thunderbolt 5, which will allow customers to run multiple Mac Studios in a cluster with shared memory to distribute inference across machines. And, according to Apple, a cluster of four Mac Studios yields three times the performance of a single Mac Studio.

Speaking from personal experience, I know that my M3 Ultra Mac Studio using oMLX can run DeepSeek-V4-Flash locally with generation averaging 35 tokens/second. Assuming a linear 4x increase, that would put the same model at over 120 tokens/second on an M5 Ultra Mac Studio.

To put things in perspective, that kind of performance would be faster than any AI chatbot website, it’d be faster than many providers who offer a “fast” mode for their models, and it’d only be second to either dedicated NVIDIA PC clusters at home or specialized inference providers such as Cerebras or Groq …which are running in full-blown data centers.

Sure, you would need a computer that is likely going to cost more than $20,000 to make it happen, but it’d still be possible on a single machine that is small, quiet, and that – in theory – any consumer can buy off the shelf.

It’s also interesting to consider the implications of M5 Ultra for running much larger models that would have typically required aggressive quantization to even stay in memory and produce any useful output. For example, Z. ai’s GLM-5.

2 (a 744B MoE model) could run at up to 17 tokens/second on an M3 Ultra Mac Studio with 512 GB of RAM; the same person was even able to get the massive Kimi K3 model to run on a single machine…with decoding performance up to 3 tokens/second.

During the WWDC26 keynote, Apple announced its third generation of Apple Foundation Models (AFM), comprising five models, some of which are local, some of which are cloud-based, and one of which lives in Google’s servers running on Nvidia chips. Here’s a breakdown of how that will work.

A bit of background

When Apple first announced its foundation models in 2024, the lineup included an on-device language model with roughly 3 billion parameters, and “a larger server-based language model available with Private Cloud Compute and running on Apple silicon servers,” as the company put it at the time.

Private Cloud Compute was an ambitious undertaking, as it aimed to deliver cloud-based AI capabilities while preserving the same privacy guarantees users expect from on-device processing.

For this reason, keeping everything in-house was essential. Private Cloud Compute ran in Apple data centers, on servers powered by Apple silicon. Even so, its privacy guarantees could be independently verified by third-party security researchers.

However, as Apple struggled to get its AI aspirations off the ground, the company partnered with Google to use Gemini as the backbone of its new AI efforts, the results of which it announced earlier this week during the WWDC26 keynote.

Apple’s new foundation models

The third generation of AFMs includes five models: AFM 3 Core and AFM 3 Code Advanced, which are on-device models, and AFM Cloud, ADM 3 Cloud (Image), and AFM 3 Cloud Pro, which are server-based. The D in ADM 3 Cloud (Image) stands for diffusion, a technology we’ve covered in the past here.

Except for AFM 3 Cloud Pro, all other models were built to run on Apple silicon devices. AFM 3 Cloud Pro, meanwhile, runs on NVIDIA GPUs hosted in Google Cloud.

This was made possible afer Apple extended its Private Cloud Compute architecture to third-party infrastructure for the first time, “while maintaining Apple’s powerful security and privacy protections,” according to the company.

As for the models themselves, here’s a breakdown of each one, as explained by Apple:

AFM 3 Core, the next generation of our 3-billion-parameter dense model that delivers a step up in quality. AFM 3 Core Advanced, our most powerful on-device model. It’s natively multimodal, enabling helpful features like expressive voices and higher-accuracy dictation.

Built on cutting-edge Apple research, this 20-billion-parameter model uses a sparse architecture, activating just 1 to 4 billion parameters at a time depending on the request. AFM 3 Core Advanced is unlocked by and optimized for our most capable Apple silicon systems. AFM 3 Cloud, our server-side workhorse, optimized for speed, efficiency, and performance.

ADM 3 Cloud (Image), for image generation and editing, which unlocks advanced photo-editing tools, the all-new Image Playground, and more. AFM 3 Cloud Pro, our most capable server-based model, which powers our most demanding use cases, like agentic tool use and complex reasoning.

articles.title: Caches and purging in macOS Tahoe
articles.subtitle: Caching to disk improves performance, but cached data are optional and may to purged when additional free space is needed. This explains how that's performed by the deleted service.
articles.author: The Eclectic Light Company
articles.content:
We judge our Macs on the responsiveness of their graphical interface. Open a folder of images in a Finder Gallery view and start scrolling through its contents. If each image preview took a couple of seconds to render, we’d be unhappy at that sluggish performance. For QuickLook to generate each preview image whenever it needs to be rendered would take time and plenty of computing power. The solution is to generate each preview once, and to cache those images both on disk and in memory.

Caching data to disk is one of the tasks common to many components in macOS, including apps like Safari and Mail. As with third-party apps, each has to manage its own caches, tracking how much space they’re using, and ensuring that’s used effectively without running free disk space too low.

Those disk caches are optional extras, and when macOS needs to find additional free space they’re candidates for deletion, or purging, along with other non-essential features such as local snapshots made by Time Machine. The disk space that could be freed by their removal is thus considered to be purgeable space, and is managed by the deleted service in the subsystem com.apple.cache_delete.

deleted only manages the caching services listed in the property lists in /System/Library/CacheDelete. As that’s in the SSV it can’t be modified or added to, so third-party apps that want their caches to be included can set the isPurgeable flag on those files to true to add them to the com.apple.fspurgeable_data list.

Each caching service keeps an account of its cached files and the total space they take, some periodically refreshing that using a background service scheduled and dispatched by DAS-CTS. When deleted needs to know how much space could be freed by purging those caches, it obtains the current figure from each of those services in turn.

It can then work out whether sufficient space could be purged to meet a request from macOS, thus whether that request can be accommodated by realising purgeable space. If it can, it’s then up to deleted to call for the selected caching services to purge their caches to provide the free space needed.

When a request is made to deleted to free purgeable space to enable an operation such as copying a file into the volume, you’ll see a succession of entries like 0.654212 com.apple.cache_delete com.apple.fspurgeable_data: 0 giving the purgeable space available for each caching service. For example, when there are Time Machine snapshots that could be purged, its log entry might read 0.654500 com.apple.cache_delete com.apple.TMCacheDelete: 94876508160

Those are totalled in 0.654501 com.apple.cache_delete CACHE_DELETE_SHARED_PURGEABLE: 94876508160 and summarised in the entries 00.654638 com.apple.cache_delete << 0.654770 com.apple.cache_delete CACHE_DELETE_TOTAL_AVAILABLE: 94876561408

If the decision is made to proceed with the purging, that’s recorded with entries listing the caching services to be used: 0.657438 com.apple.cache_delete PurgeOperation on volume [private], registered services: 0.657438 com.apple.cache_delete com.apple.TMCacheDelete 0.657439 com.apple.cache_delete com.apple.deleted_helper

The purge is then started with the information 0.658195 com.apple.cache_delete urgencyLimit: 3, info at start: { "CACHE_DELETE_AMOUNT" = 7707074560; "CACHE_DELETE_CALLING_PROCESS" = Finder; "CACHE_DELETE_FREESPACE_GOAL" = 12893556736; "CACHE_DELETE_ID" = "com.apple.cache_delete"; "CACHE_DELETE_MEASURE_ELAPSED_TIME" = 0; "CACHE_DELETE_QOS" = 25; "CACHE_DELETE_TOKEN" = "C58DB946-8B85-42AF-9291-0D8AF092002E"; "CACHE_DELETE_URGENCY_LIMIT" = 3; "CACHE_DELETE_VOLUME" = "/Volumes/TestVolume1";}

In this case, purging snapshots takes several seconds work by APFS, during which deleted continues to monitor purgeable and free space. When that’s complete it writes an entry to summarise the result 9.616316 com.apple.cache_delete Purge Result: 94876618752 bytes on: [CacheDeleteDaemonVolume] at: /Volumes/TestVolume1 [/dev/disk7s1: apfs] freespace: 100063100928 (100.06 GB), initialFreespace: 5186482176 (5.19 GB), used: 1048576 (1.05 MB), total size: 100189175808 (100.19 GB)PRIMARY, diskRef: 0xc39018a20

In other cases, purging sufficient space may require a series of phases run at different levels of urgency, starting at 3, and targeting groups of caching services, until sufficient free space has been created to complete the action that needed the additional free space.

There are some occasions when, even though there’s ample free space, multiple rounds of purging may be undertaken. One of the most obvious is when installing a macOS update.

Many apps and services in macOS cache data to disk to improve performance.

Cached data is optional, so when additional free space is needed, it may be purged, thus accounting for purgeable space. This can also include any Time Machine local snapshots.

Each caching service maintains accounts of its caches and the space they occupy.

When purgeable space is required, deleted (subsystem com.apple.cache_delete) first discovers purgeable space for each caching service, to determine whether it’s sufficient.

If it is, and the decision is taken to purge caches, caching services are called on to free up space by purging their caches as required.

articles.title: Apple finally hits a VR home run
articles.subtitle: Macworld I’ve never had a desire to buy a Vision Pro. Even if I had $4,000 to blow at the Apple Store, I’d probably pick up a loaded MacBook Pro or a Mac mini with a Studio Display XDR instead of Apple’s cutting-edge handset.
articles.author: Macworld Reviews
articles.content:
I’ve never had a desire to buy a Vision Pro. Even if I had $4,000 to blow at the Apple Store, I’d probably pick up a loaded MacBook Pro or a Mac mini with a Studio Display XDR instead of Apple’s cutting-edge handset.

But Friday Night Baseball in Apple Immersive changed my perspective. The first-ever broadcast of a live Major League Baseball game with 3D video recorded in 8K with a 180-degree field of view, watching the Red Sox-Yankees game on the Vision Pro was almost as breathtaking as being at Yankee Stadium. Even if I was able to take screenshots of the experience, it wouldn’t have done it justice. It’s literally the kind of thing you need to see to believe.

Most of the time I was watching the game from just beside the dugout of the team that was batting. I could turn to see the on-deck batter warming up, watch the pitch come in, and see the whole park in front of me. As usual for Apple’s Friday Night Baseball, the picture quality was outstanding, from the on-field action to the footprints and sunflower seeds in the dirt below my view.

I’ve visitied many baseball stadiums and sat in all kinds of seats, but nothing compared to the immersive view Apple provided. You can get a sense of it in the post below, but a flat image doesn’t really do it justice.

While the camera put me inside the stadium, the broadcast still let me know that I was watching Apple TV. Paul Severino and Xavier Scruggs were the dedicated announcers (different from the ones on the Apple TV broadcast), and they often reminded viewers that they were witnessing something special. If I looked up, I could watch the flat Apple TV scoreboard and see relevant stats.

Live immersive MLB on Apple Vision Pro. It felt like I was at Yankee Stadium. The whole experience was incredible. Shot through the lens with iPhone since it can’t be recorded on headset. pic.twitter.com/oF1J9tBTd8 — Justin Ryan (@justinryanio) August 29, 2026

Live immersive MLB on Apple Vision Pro. It felt like I was at Yankee Stadium. The whole experience was incredible. Shot through the lens with iPhone since it can’t be recorded on headset. pic.twitter.com/oF1J9tBTd8

There were a few replays that were particularly impressive, including Ben Rice’s first-inning double that made it feel like I was practically playing left field. I was so close to the action that I could hear muffled chatter in the dugout and see sunflowseeds spit in my direction.

Between innings was particularly magical. There were no commercials, so the view stayed in the stadium, with the camera shifting to the broadcast booth above home plate numerous times to get an expansive overhead view of the whole field. And when David Bednar came in to close the ninth inning, the camera view shifted to center field so I could see his full bullpen entrance and watch him jog to the pitcher’s mound while his walkout song, Styx’s “Renegade,” played in the stadium.

It was so enthralling, I wanted a way to mute the broadcast to soak in the sounds of the stadium. It wasn’t so much that the announcers were bad (though Apple TV has never been known for its broadcast crew), but the Spatial Audio microphones were so clear that the ambiance of the ballpark was enough.

Unfortunately, the game ended 1-0, so there wasn’t a ton of action other than a solo home run, but one particular play stands out as a showcase for what the immersive broadcast brings. In the top of the 7th inning, the Red Sox loaded the bases with one out, so I strapped on my Vision Pro to watch the rest of the inning.

It only took two pitches to end the Red Sox threat. Wilson Contreras hit a fly ball to left field that was caught by Cody Bellinger, who fired the ball home to get a tagging-up Ceddanne Rafaela and end the inning. Watching the play unfold and turning to watch the throw reach home was incredible and better than any TV broadcast I’ve ever watched.

A near homerun

As we wrote in our review, Vision Pro is a pretty heavy device, so keeping it strapped on for two-plus hours isn’t ideal. I don’t have the Dual Knit Band, which might help, but as it was, I watched the game in spurts. I took it off after the first three innings and then returned to it whenever there was a runner in scoring position.

There’s also the issue of eye strain. I have prescription lenses for the Vision Pro, which could exacerbate the issue, but my eyes quickly get tired when using Vision Pro. This was compounded by the sheer immersiveness of the picture that didn’t give my eyes any time to rest.

But I’m already looking forward to the next game on Friday between the L.A. Angels and Pittsburgh Pirates. It’s a shame Vision Pro is so expensive, because every baseball fan should experience it. Maybe Apple can sell Vision Pro tickets next season and start selling hot dogs at the Apple Store. Learn more about the Apple Vision Pro.

articles.subtitle: Macworld USB-C and its Thunderbolt variant are the most up-to-date standards of the USB connector. They allow data-transfer speeds of up to 80Gbps, can fast-charge devices up to 240W, and conveniently fit in a port either way up—which means that you can...
articles.author: Macworld Reviews
articles.content:
USB-C and its Thunderbolt variant are the most up-to-date standards of the USB connector. They allow data-transfer speeds of up to 80Gbps, can fast-charge devices up to 240W, and conveniently fit in a port either way up—which means that you can wave bye-bye to the age-old USB guessing game of “Which way does it go in?”.

USB-C is no one-trick pony—handling data transfer, video output and power input. You’ll find faster variants of USB-C (called Thunderbolt 3, 4 or 5) on Macs. Each version of Thunderbolt is backwards compatible with USB-C so the adapters reviewed here will all work with modern Macs—from the MacBooks Neo, Air and Pro, through to the desktop iMac, Mac mini and Studio.

USB-C’s 5-10Gbps speeds will limit some of Thunderbolt’s more impressive 40 to 80Gbps potential but for most people even 5Gbps is fast enough. If super-fast data transfer is one of your requirements, a number of hubs reviewed below do use Thunderbolt or 40Gbps USB4.

Find out more in our Thunderbolt 5 vs Thunderbolt 4 vs Thunderbolt 3 comparison and also our chart at the end showing all the ports of Apple’s recent Macs.

Apple

In general, an “ adapter ” works with a single port (such as USB-A or Ethernet) while a “ hub ” gives you multiple ports. If you require even more, then look for a “ docking station ” or “ dock “. Docks usually come with their own power supply, while hubs require a separate USB-C charger if you need a power source. If you’re after a full desktop setup for your MacBook, look out for our recommendations for the best USB-C and Thunderbolt docking stations for MacBooks.

Apple sells its own range of USB-C adapters to HDMI, VGA and more, but they are overpriced and underpowered compared to the premium USB-C hubs and adapters we have reviewed here. We haven’t included the many much cheaper but lower-quality versions you can find online as we recommend only from trusted and tested makers.

Look for each hub’s video capability for connecting to external displays. Most support only one monitor, but some offer two—note that more than two usually requires an extra software install.

Passthrough power will likely also be of interest to MacBook users. 60W Power Delivery (PD) will work even for the 16-inch MacBook Pro (just), but more watts equals a faster charge.

Note that the ports on the MacBook Neo are USB-C and only one of them is properly data-ready at 10Gbps, with the other just for charging. Read more on how the MacBook Neo’s USB-C ports are different. As it has just one data port, a USB-C hub becomes a must for expanding the Neo’s potential—read our roundup of the best MacBook Neo accessories.
